data.title: The Bavarian Geographer – the first written mention of the Slavs of Nitra
data.excerpt: The Bavarian Geographer (in Latin Geographus Bavarus) is the conventional name that Jan Potocki gave in 1796 to the author of an anonymous medieval document, Descriptio civitatum et regionum ad septentrionalem plagam Danubii, discovered in 1772 in the Bavarian State Library in Munich. Among the Slavic tribes its 9th-century list names the Merehani with their 30 hillforts – and renowned historians read them as the Slavs of Nitra, the direct ancestors of today’s Slovaks.
data.metaTitle: The Bavarian Geographer and the Slavs of Nitra
data.metaDescription: The anonymous 9th-century document of the Bavarian Geographer, Descriptio civitatum, carries one of the first written mentions of the Slavs of Nitra.

timeline.title: The Descriptio civitatum is composed
timeline.description: An unknown author, probably working in the monastery of Reichenau, Fulda or Regensburg, compiled a list of Slavic tribes and of the number of their hillforts between the Elbe, the Danube, the Volga and the Black Sea.

timeline.title: The union of the Moravians and the Nitrans
timeline.description: According to the interpretation of J. Stanislav and other scholars, around this year Mojmír united the Moravian (Marharii) and the Nitra (Merehani) principality into a single whole.

timeline.title: Additions to the text in Regensburg
timeline.description: According to one hypothesis, around this year additions made in the monastery of St Emmeram in Regensburg were appended to the original list from Fulda.

timeline.title: Discovery of the document
timeline.description: The brief manuscript was discovered in the Bavarian State Library in Munich.

timeline.title: The name ‘Bavarian Geographer’
timeline.description: Jan Potocki gave the anonymous author of the document the conventional name Geographus Bavarus – the Bavarian Geographer.

children.text: The Bavarian Geographer (in Latin Geographus Bavarus) is the conventional name that Jan Potocki gave in 1796 to the author of an anonymous medieval document, Descriptio civitatum et regionum ad septentrionalem plagam Danubii (“
A description of the towns and regions on the northern bank of the Danube
”). The brief document was discovered in 1772 in the Bavarian State Library in Munich.
The 9th-century document contains a list of tribes in the east of Central Europe

, between the Elbe, the Danube, the Volga and the Black Sea. For the most part these are Slavic tribes. It also contains information on the number of civitates (towns, strongholds and hillforts) controlled by the individual tribes. The interpretation of this source is not unambiguous, because it is very difficult to identify the Latin names of the tribes.

The origin of the document has not yet been satisfactorily clarified. The first scholars placed it in Regensburg or Salzburg; today it is attributed rather to the Swabian monastery of Reichenau. According to one hypothesis the list was compiled by St Methodius, who in the 870s probably stayed at Reichenau and could have been connected with his mission in the Slavic lands. Another possible author is the monastic librarian Reginbertinus, who was probably active in the 830s to 850s. According to another theory it arose in the first half of the 9th century at Fulda at the instigation of the East Frankish king Louis the German, and around the year 845 additions made in the monastery of St Emmeram in Regensburg were appended to it. Scholars assume that the list consists of two parts, which may be dated to different periods and attributed to different authors.

children.text: Why is this work so important for us? Because here, in the 9th century, the Bavarian Geographer
mentions, among other peoples, certain ‘Merehanos
’ who at that time had 30 hillforts, and
these Merehanos are the Slavs of Nitra, the Sloveni – or, if you like, the ancestors of today’s Slovaks

. It is thus the oldest document in which our Slovak ancestors are mentioned, and we are in the time of Great Moravia. We can see that, long after the union of Moravia with the Nitra region, the Bavarian Geographer still perceived a difference between the original Moravians and the ‘other Moravians’ (in reality the Nitrans) – unfortunately he does not call them by the term we would wish, the Nitrans, but he nevertheless clearly distinguishes them.

Are you saying I have now overshot a little? Then let us look at what two renowned historians have to say on the subject, neither of whom is any kind of flag-waving nationalist; on questions of our history they are rather sceptics. First of all, let us look at a quotation from the
book
by the Czech historian
Dušan Třeštík
, Vznik Velké Moravy (The Rise of Great Moravia).
On page 132 he states:
One ethno-political name could, however, perhaps be applied to Slovakia.
It is given by the author of the so-called Bavarian Geographer, but
as Merehani

– that is, evidently the Moravians. (…) In the first part the gentes are enumerated from the Obodrites in the north southwards. After the Boheman-Czechs (Beheimare) the Moravians (Marharii) are correctly placed, but then the Bulgarians are spoken of, and again certain ‘Moravians’ - Merehani. With that the list of frontier gentes ends, and the second part, which covers those ‘who sit beyond them’, begins with the Danubian Obodrites of whom we spoke above. In the case of the Merehani the inhabitants of the basin of the Serbian Morava (the right-hand, that is southern, tributary of the Danube) can certainly not be considered here – as the geographical order would suggest – because the geographer adheres consistently to his programme and really always lists only the gentes sitting north of the Danube. That the ‘Marharii’ are the Moravians no one has ever doubted, just as it has always been quite generally accepted that the ‘vulgarite’ are the Bulgarians. The question has always been who those ‘Merehani’ are, placed evidently somewhere in this space between the Morava and the region of the Iron Gates or Belgrade. The localisation of these Merehani between the Dyje and the Danube, which has also been considered rather often, is out of the question, because in the first half of the 9th century Slavic occupation here was only very sparse and certainly no gens could have lived here together. Relatively dense Slavic occupation was to be found only on the right bank of the Danube, between Vienna and Mautern, that is in ‘Avaria’ within the territory of the empire. But since the Obodrites evidently sat on the lower Tisza,
that effectively leaves only Slovakia for the localisation of the Merehani
. This has also been considered most often. In that case the pair Marhari-Merehani would probably be two parts of the Moravian state, the Moravian and the Nitran, named by variants of a shared name.”
Ján Steinhübel

, who likewise can certainly not be reproached with any excessive nationalism, states quite unambiguously and without hesitation in his book Nitrianske kniežatstvo (The Principality of Nitra) that the Merehanos mentioned are the Nitrans. Among other things, on pages 89–91 he writes that “
the Bavarian author, who summarised his knowledge of the Slavic lands on the borders of the new East Frankish Empire,
clearly distinguishes the two Great Moravian principalities

(…) This work arose about 10 years after the conquest of the Nitra region by Mojmír. For foreign observers, therefore, the inhabitants of both principalities are already Moravians. Our unknown author expressed the difference between them by a variation in the name.
The nearer ones he called Marharii, and the more distant ones, whom he still regarded as a separate ‘people – populus’, Merehani.

Before the year 833, however, the Slavs of Nitra could not have been called Moravians, because the Morava, from which the Moravians and their whole principality took their name, did not flow through the Nitra region. The princely stronghold and the principality of Nitrava took their name from the river Nitrava. If, therefore, we may continue the analogy Morava – Nitrava, we arrive at a further analogy, Moravians – Nitravians. Just as the inhabitants of the principality of Morava, so exactly
the inhabitants of the principality of Nitrava could have been the Nitravians

. The Czechs, Serbs, Croats, Obodrites, Dudlebes and other ancient tribes bore their name from time immemorial; they kept it even after being divided into two (or even three) smaller tribes, and it remained with them even after they occupied new territory. The presumed Nitravians, like the Moravians, however, belonged to those tribes which, in the words of the Russian chronicler Nestor, named themselves by their own names (according to) where they settled, in which place.
In the time of its independence the principality of Nitrava lay outside the attention of the chroniclers of the day, and so they did not record even the name of the presumed Nitravians”.
Next I shall quote the eminent Slovak linguist and Slavist
Ján Stanislav
, who in his work Starosloviensky jazyk (The Old Church Slavonic Language) states that

“Interpretations of this record differ. It is thought that the Marharii were the Slavs between the Danube, the Dyje, the Morava and the White Carpathians, and that they were united by Mojmír or his predecessor.
The Merehani would be their kinsmen between the Danube and the Carpathians, with their centre in Nitra

. This formation was united by Pribina or his predecessor. Both formations were united by Mojmír around the year 833. This is how the record is most recently explained by Fr. Dvorník (Byzant. misie 93–94). He cited the view of L. Havlík, according to whom the Bavarian Geographer did not intend the names Marharii and Merehani to denote two different tribes, but two different political formations of the same tribe, which arose around two independent centres.”
Finally, we cannot pass over the important contribution of
Drahoslav Hulínek
, who in the well-regarded edited volume Bitka pri Bratislave (The Battle of Bratislava), on page 198, states that
“Despite these facts
(the problem of dating the hillforts in Slovakia – note by Orgoň)
we may assume a certain increase in the founding of hillforts from the second third of the 9th century, which is confirmed by the above-mentioned account of the so-called Bavarian Geographer.
The mention of 30 strongholds suggests a relatively dense distribution of hillforts.
On the basis of the present state of archaeological confirmation we may, for the 9th century – after its first third –
assume that at least some 35–40 hillforts existed in the territory of western and central Slovakia.
… On the basis of similar archaeological and statistical criteria we may assume that in Moravia, within the present state borders, there were 15–20 fortified settlements…
The ratio, within the range of the number of hillforts I have so far assumed, between the Moravian and the Nitran parts of Great Moravia
to a certain extent only hypothetically
corresponds to the data in the work of the Bavarian Geographer,
where, on the basis of J. Steinhübel’s interpretations, this ratio approaches a level of around 1:3, or a range of 1:2 to 1:3.”

children.text: As you can see, renowned historians and linguists too believe that in the 9th century the Bavarian Geographer listed our direct ancestors among the other Slavic tribes, naming them by a separate term. The word ‘Sloven’ or ‘Slovák’ is not there? But neither is the word ‘Čech’. Note that our western brothers too are named here as
Betheimare,

which is not derived from the ethnic name of a Slavic tribe but from the territory that had previously belonged to the Celtic Boii. Even so, this term is automatically translated as ‘the Czechs’. So let us not throw away such wonderful documents either, and let us realise that the term Slovak is simply not to be found in the 9th century – but our ancestors are.
The literal translation of the Bavarian Geographer reads as follows:
A description of the towns and regions on the northern bank of the Danube.

blocks.text: These are they who dwell nearest to the borders of the Danes; they are called Nortabtrezi [3] - there is a region in which there are 53 towns, divided among their princes. Vuilci [4], where there are 95 towns and four regions. Lina [5] is a people which has 7 towns. Near them dwell those whom they call Bethenici, Smeldingon and Morizani [6], who have 11 towns. Beside them are those who are called Hehfeldi [7] and who have 8 towns. Beside them is a region which they call Surb [8]; in such a region there are several (districts), and it has 50 towns. Beside them are those whom they call Talaminzi [9], who have 14 towns. Betheimare [Becheimare] [10], among whom there are 15 towns. Marharii [11] have 11 towns. Vulgarite [12] have extensive lands and a numerous people, having 5 towns; for they are a great multitude and it is not their custom to have towns. There is a people whom they call Merehani [13]; these have 30 towns. These are the regions which border on our own lands. These are they who dwell beside these lands: Osterabtrezi [14], where there are more than 100 towns, Miloxi [15], where there are 67 towns. Phesnuzi [15] have 70 towns. Tlaidesi [15] have more than 200 towns. Glopeani [16], among whom there are 400 towns or even more. Zuireani [17] have 325 towns. Busan [18] have 231 towns. Sittici [15], a region immeasurable in its people and its most strongly fortified towns. Stadici [15], among whom there are 516 towns and a countless people. Sebbirozi [15] have 90 towns. Unlizi [19], a numerous people, 318 towns. Neriuani [15] have 78 towns. Artorozi [15] have 145, a people (that is) very tough. Epataradici [15] have 263 towns. Vuillerozi [15] have 180 towns. Zabrozi [15] have 212 towns. Znetalici [15] have 74 towns. Aturezani [15] have 104 towns. Chozirozi [15] have 250 towns. Lendizi [20] have 98 towns. Thafnezi [15] have 257 towns. Zeriuani [15], which is such a kingdom that from it all the peoples of the Slavs originate and derive their origin, as they affirm. Prissani [21] (have) 70 towns. Velunzani [22] 70 towns. BRUZ [23] are on all sides more extensive than (the distance) from the Enns to the Rhine. Vuizunbeire [15]. Caziri [24] 100 towns. Ruzzi [25], Forsderen liudi [15], Fresiti [15], Serauici [15], Lucolane [15], Ungaro [26], Vuislane [27], Sleenzane [28] 15 towns. Lunsizi [29] 30 towns. Dadosesani [30] 20 towns. Milzane [31] 30 towns. Besunzane [32] 2 towns, Verizane [15] 10 towns. Fraganeo [15] 40 towns. Lupiglaa [15] 30 towns. Opolini [33] 20 towns. Golensizi [34] 5 towns.

The Latin text of the Descriptio:
Descriptio ciuitatum et regionum ad septentrionalem plagam Danubii.

blocks.text: Isti sunt qui propinquiores resident finibus Danaorum quos uocant Nortabtrezi ubi regio in qua sunt ciuitates LIII per ducos partitae. Vuilci in qua ciuitates XCV et regiones IIII. Linaa est populus qui habet ciuitates VII. prope illis resident quas uocant Bethenici, et Smeldingon, et Morizani, qui habent ciuitates XI. Iuxta illos sunt qui uocantur Hehfeldi, qui habent civitates VIII. Iuxta illos est regio, quae uocatur Surbi. in qua regione plures sunt quae ha bent ciuitates L. Iuxta illos sunt quos uocantur Talaminzi, qui habent civitates XIIII. Betheimare in qua sunt civitates XV. Marharii habent ciuitates XI. Vulgarii regio est inmensa et populus multus habens ciuitates V. eo quod multitudo magna ex eis sit et non sit eis opus ciuitates habere. Est populus quem uocant Merehanos, ipsi habent ciuitates XXX. Iste sunt regiones quae terminant in finibus nostris. Isti sunt qui iuxta istorum fines resident. Osterabtrezi, in qua ciuitates plusquam C sunt. Miloxi, in qua ciuitates LXVII. Phesnuzi habent ciuitates LXX. Thadesi plusquam CC urbes habent. Glopeani, in qua ciuitates CCCC aut eo amplius. Zuireani habent ciuitates CCCXXV. Busani habent ciuitates CCXXXI. Sittici regio inmensa populis et urbibus munitissimis. Stadici in qua ciuitates DXVI populusque infinitus. Sebbirozi habent ciuitates XC. Vnlizi, populus multus, ciuitates CCCXVIII. Neriuani habent ciuitates LXXVIII. Attorozi habent CXL VIII, populus ferocissimus. Eptaradici habent ciuitates CCLXIII. Vuillerozi habent ciuitates CLXXX. Zabrozi habent ciuitates CCXII. Znetalici habent ciuitates LXXIIlI. Aturezani habent ciuitates CIIII. Chozirozi habent ciuitates CCL. Lendizi habent ciuitates XCVIII. Thafnezi habent ciuitates CCLVII. Zeriuani quod tantum est regnum ut ex eo cunctae gentes Sclauorum exortae sint et originem sicut affirmant ducant. Prissani ciuitates LXX. Velunzani ciuitates LXX. Bruzi plus est undique quam de Enisa ad Rhenum. Vuizunbeire. Caziri ciuitates C. Ruzzi. Forsderen. Liudi. Fresiti. Serauici. Lucolane. Vngare. Vuislane. Sleenzane ciuitates XV. Lunsizi ciuitates XXX. Dadosesani ciuitates XX. Milzane ciuitates XXX. Besunzane ciuitates II. Verizane ciuitates X. Fraganeo ciuitates XL. Lupiglaa ciuitates XXX. Opolini ciuitates XX. Golensizi ciuitates V. Sueui non sunt nati, sed seminati. Beire non dicuntur bauarii, sed boiarii, a boia fluvio.
